candidates.title: The improv rule the episode is named after
candidates.detail: Alice tries saying yes to everything and it collapses under its own weight. Ted and Beard give her the improviser's version instead: accept what you are handed, then add something of your own. The principle is standard improv-theatre practice, but its authorship is genuinely murky. The usual lineage runs through the Compass Players' 'Kitchen Rules' in the 1950s (David Shepherd and Paul Sills), Viola Spolin's idea of group agreement, and Del Close, a Spolin student who taught the 'yes, and' formulation and named a production company Yes And with Charna Halpern in the 1980s. Spolin's own estate says the phrase is not formally in her Improvisation for the Theater, and none of the standard histories credit a single coiner.
candidates.moment: Alice's blanket-yes approach snarls up a training session; Ted and Beard take her aside and hand her the two-word upgrade.

candidates.title: Where the say-yes-to-everything advice comes from
candidates.detail: Reviewers do not agree on what Alice is actually following. TVLine and Ready Steady Cut describe a self-help tape; the A.V. Club calls it a grindset guru online; Lady Geeks and Comic Basics just say a motivational speaker. No source reports the show naming a source on screen. Worth flagging for the reviewer: the best-known version of the doctrine is Danny Wallace's 2005 memoir Yes Man, a year of saying yes to every offer, loosely adapted into the 2008 Jim Carrey film. There is no evidence the episode references Wallace, and the card must not claim it does.
candidates.moment: Alice arrives back from suspension committed to agreeing with everything put in front of her.

candidates.title: The sign meets a room it does not answer
candidates.detail: The BELIEVE sign goes up in the women's changing room and the players push back: they already believe. What is in their way is childcare, rent, a car that will not start, a second job. Multiple reviewers read this as the season turning its own slogan over and finding the limit of it — optimism as a strategy works differently for people whose problems are material. Ready Steady Cut headlined its recap on exactly this point.
candidates.moment: The sign is hung; the room's response is that belief is not the thing they are short of.

candidates.title: Two more words on a Post-it
candidates.detail: Alice answers the room not by defending the sign but by amending it — a Post-it adding a second clause about winning. Reviewers describe the moment landing when Lizzie's young son reads the amended sign aloud. The gesture makes the borrowed sign the women's own rather than a hand-me-down from the men's side; it is also, structurally, a 'yes, and' applied to Ted's own creed.

candidates.title: The song over the opening montage
candidates.detail: The cold-open montage of the players' ordinary mornings runs under TLC's 'Unpretty' (1999, from FanMail). The song was co-written by Tionne 'T-Boz' Watkins and Dallas Austin from a poem Watkins wrote and published in her collection Thoughts, written while she was in and out of intensive care with complications from sickle-cell anaemia. Its subject is the gap between what you are worth and what you are told you are worth — which is the episode's whole argument, transposed from bodies to paycheques.
candidates.moment: Before the title card: childcare falling through, rent going up, a car that will not start, a delivery shift, all scored to the TLC track.

candidates.title: What the women's team is actually asking for
candidates.detail: The players confront Ted over pay: their popularity is not reaching their wages. Reviewers note the men's side has never had to hold this conversation. Real-world anchor, kept separate from the fiction: English women's football only reached full-time salaries league-wide from the 2025-26 season, when the Women's Super League and WSL2 introduced minimum salary requirements developed with the Professional Footballers' Association. Reported WSL wages still range from roughly £20,000-£27,000 at smaller clubs to £40,000-£60,000 for regular squad players at the bigger ones. The show never states which league Richmond's women play in, so the comparison is context, not a claim about the fiction.
candidates.moment: The squad puts the pay question to Ted directly rather than to the club.

candidates.title: Roy's entrance music is a line from Milton
candidates.detail: Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds' 'Red Right Hand' (1994, Let Love In) plays as Roy rolls in on his mobility scooter. Cave took the title from Paradise Lost, Book II, where Belial imagines God's vengeance reaching down for the fallen angels — Milton's phrase for divine retribution. Scoring a knee-injured man on a scooter to the sound of the wrath of God is the joke; it is also the show's standard move of giving Roy an aura several sizes larger than his circumstances.

candidates.title: Beard buys a new face
candidates.detail: Beard turns up altered — a spray tan and blue contact lenses — after being called old on New Year's Eve. Reviewers describe it as an ego death followed by a reinvention aimed at the wrong layer. It rhymes directly with the opening song: the chorus of 'Unpretty' is about buying the fix rather than addressing the hurt, and Beard is the episode's literal demonstration of it.
candidates.moment: Beard arrives at work visibly changed, and the change fools nobody.

In each of the first two they played potential love interests. The A.V. Club flags SuperBob specifically in its recap of this episode, the one in which the relationship ends.

candidates.title: A break-up conducted as an act of accuracy
candidates.detail: Dr. Erin ends the relationship herself, on the grounds that Roy is still in love with Keeley — a fact she says he let slip while medicated at New Year. She does not argue or bargain; she names what is true and releases him, framing it as his deserving to be with the person he loves. It is the rare TV break-up where the person with less power in the scene is the one being honest.
candidates.moment: Erin tells Roy what she has worked out and ends things on her own terms.

candidates.title: The three words Ted puts on the profile
candidates.detail: Pressed to describe himself for a dating profile, Ted lands on being lovable — and then asks out the stage manager in person and is turned down, because she is already seeing someone. The episode deliberately declines to make the claim contingent on the result. Reviewers read the willingness to ask as the growth, not the answer he gets.

candidates.title: Dolly Partonberg, agent, of Chicago
candidates.detail: To call the bluff of Dani Rojas's agent, Zelda invents a rival agent from Chicago under the name Dolly Partonberg and gathers intel in character. It works, and Rebecca makes her a special advisor at the club. Chicago is also where Ted Lasso's own performers come from — the character was built by Jason Sudeikis, Brendan Hunt and Joe Kelly out of Chicago-school improv — which makes the fake city a quiet fit for an episode about 'yes, and'.
